Wright State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 23-11 overall and 15-5 in Horizon League play, then added the Horizon League tournament title with a 103-90 semifinal win over Northern Kentucky on March 9, 2026 and a 66-63 championship win over Detroit Mercy on March 10, 2026. The Raiders won the regular-season title outright before the conference tournament and finished first in the league standings. Team cumulative numbers show Wright State scoring 80.7 points per game and allowing 73.4 across 34 games, a profile that matches a team built around pace, paint pressure, and turnover creation rather than slow-down possession control.

Offensively, Wright State still looks like a Clint Sargent team in the traditional Raider mold: play fast, get downhill early, and create offense through attacking guards feeding interior finishers. Sargent said before the season that he planned to “keep speedy pace of play,” and the 2025-26 numbers support that identity. The Raiders shot 48.8 percent from the floor as a team, made 241 threes, and averaged 469 assists on 975 made field goals, which indicates a real preference for drive-and-kick and interior touch passing rather than pure isolation basketball. Their roster construction shows the shape of the scheme. Michael Cooper leads them with 13.4 points per game, TJ Burch adds 12.3, and Michael Imariagbe supplies 11.8 points on 58.9 percent shooting with 7.0 rebounds per game. That is a classic inside-out distribution: Cooper and Burch create pressure on the ball, Callaghan spaces the floor with 66 made threes at 38.6 percent, and Imariagbe is the primary finisher around the rim.

Specific game evidence shows how the offense functions. In the 102-90 road win at Cleveland State on February 15, Wright State scored 51 points in each half, a strong indicator of pace continuity instead of one hot stretch. In the 90-61 Horizon League quarterfinal win over Cleveland State on March 4, the Raiders broke the game open with a 17-3 run early in the second half, and five different players scored in that burst. That matters schematically: this is not one star calling his own number; it is a multi-handler attack that flows from penetration, secondary cuts, and kick-out shooting. Against Green Bay on February 1, Wright State scored 26 first-half points in the paint in an 83-75 road win, another clear sign that rim pressure is foundational. In late-clock or must-score possessions, they often trust a straight-line creator or a post touch to Imariagbe; his putback winner in the 92-91 comeback at Northern Kentucky on February 28 is the cleanest example of their commitment to crashing the glass after the first action.

Defensively, Wright State is more disruptive than dominant. The raw season totals show 252 steals and 148 blocks, and the identity starts with Burch. He won Horizon League Defensive Player of the Year and Newcomer of the Year, entered postseason play averaging 2.63 steals per game, and had 79 steals through the regular season before finishing with 83 in 33 games. Wright State’s defense is built to speed up opposing guards, jump passing lanes, and turn live-ball steals into transition offense. Their pressure is most visible on the perimeter: Burch had six steals against Oakland on December 29 and multiple steals in 20 games by March 2. They are not a shutdown half-court defense every night, though. Cleveland State scored 85 in Dayton on January 21, Detroit Mercy scored 77 in a February 12 upset at the Nutter Center, and Robert Morris held Wright State to 68 in an 81-68 win on February 22. What that reveals is a defense that can be exposed by physical guards and hot shooting if the Raiders do not control the ball. Still, when the pressure works, it changes games quickly. In the 86-58 win over Green Bay on December 7, Wright State forced 18 turnovers and recorded 14 steals, with Burch alone collecting five steals.

Sargent’s coaching philosophy is visible in both style and adjustments. He wants aggressive offense, tempo, and shared rhythm, but his most important 2025-26 improvement was getting the roster to defend with more purpose after last season’s inconsistency. The documented adjustment history is strong. After losing 85-79 at home to Cleveland State on January 21, Wright State answered in the rematch with a 102-90 road win on February 15, then crushed Cleveland State 90-61 in the league tournament on March 4. That three-game arc shows real adaptation: the Raiders gave up 85 in the first meeting, then responded by winning the next two by a combined 41 points. Similarly, after a 77-74 home loss to Detroit Mercy on February 12, they beat the Titans 66-63 in the Horizon championship on March 10. That title-game score is especially important because it shows Sargent could win a grinder after his team had been more comfortable in 80-point games all year.

Clutch and late-game execution is one of the more convincing strengths on this resume. On January 1, Wright State beat Milwaukee 76-70 by closing on a 7-2 run after the Panthers had cut the margin to 69-68 with 2:26 left. On February 25, they won 74-70 at Purdue Fort Wayne behind 24 points from Solomon Callaghan. On February 28, they produced their best late-game example: down by 20 in the second half at Northern Kentucky, they rallied all the way back and won 92-91 on Imariagbe’s tip-in with less than a second remaining. Then, in the highest-leverage game of the season, they beat Detroit Mercy 66-63 for the league title on March 10. Those are four different script types: protect a small lead, win a road grind, complete a huge comeback, and survive a championship-possession game.

The key players are well defined. Cooper, a freshman guard, is the leading scorer at 13.4 points per game with 403 total points in 30 games. He had 25 in the Horizon semifinal against Northern Kentucky on March 9, 23 against Green Bay on December 7, and 22 at Marshall on December 13. Burch is the two-way engine: 12.3 points per game, 115 assists, 83 steals, and the best on-ball defender on the roster. He scored 24 against Youngstown State on January 15, 23 against IU Indianapolis on February 19, and 19 in the 66-63 title win over Detroit Mercy on March 10. Imariagbe is the frontcourt anchor at 11.8 points and 7.0 rebounds per game while shooting 58.9 percent from the floor; he had 24 points and 11 rebounds against Northern Kentucky on January 24, 19 points and 16 rebounds against Purdue Fort Wayne on February 7, and the game-winning putback at NKU on February 28. Callaghan is the shooting specialist, making 66 threes at 38.6 percent and scoring 24 at Purdue Fort Wayne on February 25. Pickett gives them rebounding and interior length: 8.7 points, 5.4 rebounds, and 46 blocks, plus 19 points in the 92-91 win at Northern Kentucky. Bruskotter is the swing bench scorer; his 25-point outburst at Cleveland State on February 15 showed he can change a game with second-unit offense.

The notable wins tell you Wright State is dangerous when it dictates tempo. The 94-84 road win at Oakland on January 11 featured 27 from Callaghan. The 102-90 win at Cleveland State on February 15 showed the offense can travel against a team that had beaten them earlier. The 74-70 win at Purdue Fort Wayne on February 25 and the 92-91 comeback at Northern Kentucky on February 28 were championship-caliber road responses in the final week. The 103-90 semifinal over Northern Kentucky and 66-63 final over Detroit Mercy proved they could win both a track meet and a possession-by-possession title game in Indianapolis.

The notable losses are just as revealing. The 69-68 league-opening loss at Youngstown State on December 3 and the 76-74 loss at Marshall on December 13 showed early issues finishing one-possession games. The 85-79 home loss to Cleveland State on January 21 exposed defensive problems against efficient guard play. The 72-66 and 81-68 losses to Robert Morris on February 4 and February 22 suggested that physical, lower-possession teams can knock Wright State out of rhythm. The 77-74 home loss to Detroit Mercy on February 12 foreshadowed the kind of ugly game they would later have to solve in the conference final.

As for tournament coaching history, Clint Sargent is in his second season as Wright State’s head coach. His relevant NCAA tournament history as head coach is now one appearance: 2026, when he led Wright State to the Horizon League tournament championship and the automatic NCAA bid. Wright State’s last trip before that came in 2022 under Scott Nagy, not Sargent. So Sargent enters this NCAA Tournament with a 2026 résumé built on a Horizon regular-season title, a Horizon tournament title, and multiple documented in-season adjustment wins against teams that had already beaten him.

Bottom line: Wright State is a dangerous mid-major because its profile is concrete, not theoretical. The Raiders have a 23-11 record, a 15-5 league mark, 80.7 points per game, a freshman leading scorer in Cooper, a league Defensive Player of the Year in Burch, an efficient interior finisher in Imariagbe, and multiple proven late-game wins on January 1, February 25, February 28, and March 10. If they can keep the game fast and let their guards create steals and paint touches, they are capable of stressing a higher seed for 40 minutes.

The first tactical priority against Wright State is to wall off the lane and make them finish over length without living at the foul line. Their leading interior scorers tell the story. Freshman 6-foot-9 forward Kellen Pickett added 8.7 points, 5.4 rebounds, and 46 blocks, while Andrea Holden, a 6-foot-6 wing, gave them 6.3 points, 4.0 rebounds, and 40 blocks in just 14.2 minutes per game. To disrupt it, opponents need an early-gap help plan against TJ Burch and Michael Cooper, then a hard crack-down on Imariagbe and Pickett on the glass. Burch led the team with 115 assists, while Cooper and Burch combined for 810 points, so the ball starts with guard penetration and ends with frontcourt finishing or kick-outs. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/robert-morris/boxscore/10305)) Those are two concrete examples of a team shrinking the floor, keeping Wright State out of offensive rhythm, and forcing lower-efficiency jump shooting. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/robert-morris/boxscore/10305)) So the practical lesson is that token pressure is not enough; the right version is score-and-press or dead-ball pressure designed to burn clock, force Burch to initiate later, and keep Wright State from entering actions with 20-plus seconds left. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

On zone vulnerability: there is not enough reliable public possession-level tagging in the sources reviewed to claim a precise zone frequency or a named game that definitively turned on zone coverage alone. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/detroit-mercy-hl-championship-/boxscore/10359)) That suggests a compact zone can work only if it also finishes possessions; otherwise Pickett and Imariagbe will punish it on the glass. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster)) At the 2, Cooper is a sturdy 6-3 scorer at 13.4 points per game, but not a high-volume sniper by percentage, hitting 36.4% from three, so long closeouts with physical top-locking can bother him. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster)) At the 3/wing line, Pangonis at 6-7 and Holden at 6-6 can post or slash against smaller teams, while Bruskotter’s 6-8 size gives Wright State another oversized perimeter body. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster)) At the 4/5, Pickett and Imariagbe are productive but not huge by NCAA Tournament standards; Pickett is 6-9, 215 and Imariagbe is 6-7, 225, so opponents with a true 6-10-plus rim protector and a strong weakside rebounder can make their interior scoring less efficient. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/detroit-mercy-hl-championship-/boxscore/10359))

Transition tendencies are clearer. Offensively, Wright State repeatedly spikes when it can run: 17 fast-break points against Northern Kentucky in the semifinal, 12 at Northern Kentucky on February 28, 8 against Detroit Mercy in the title game, and 7 against Cleveland State. ([wsuraiders.com](https://wsuraiders.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/northern-kentucky-hl-championship-semifinal-/boxscore/10358)) Defensively, they are vulnerable when the opponent’s primary scorers get downhill before their half-court shell is set. Finally, do not play their preferred near-70-possession game unless you clearly have the better athletes.
